alternatives.transcript: One Rish session. In a moment, four Claude agents will go to work inside it. Three lanes: planning on the left, the builders in the middle, the shared board on the right. The road map agent goes first, and its very first act is to tell the board what this demo is. Then the other three check-in, standing by, nobody has been given any work yet. The road map writes the goal down, a to do manager that runs entirely in the browser. No back end, no build step, no dependencies. It posts the deliverable, then hands the whole thing to the fleet manager. That is the last order it gives. The manager splits the work by layer. Worker one takes the markup and the styling. Worker two takes all of the logic. But first, it writes a contract. The six element ids both halves must agree on. That is what stops two parallel agents from colliding. Contract posted. Now the work orders go out, one to each worker, and the build starts. Watch the middle lane. Both workers are running at once and neither has read the other's file. The contract is the only thing holding them together. Worker one is done. The page in the style sheet checked back against the contract ID by ID. Worker two finishes the logic: Add, toggle, delete, clear, completed, a live count, and the list persisted to local storage. Notice that neither worker reported back by message. They posted to the board, and the manager has been watching it because a post cannot be missed and a message can. Now the manager verifies for itself. Every ID lines up. The page loads both files. The syntax is clean. Then it signs off. The road map checks the work against its own acceptance list and closes the demo. Four agents, one board, a working app. And all four have signed off.
